research_text:
The dominant narrative around AI and time management is a trap. Every productivity dashboard, every vendor demo, every LinkedIn post sells the same promise: AI will do your busywork, and you will get your hours back. The research tells a very different, much more interesting story.

At MIT Sloan, researchers tracked what happened when Microsoft Copilot entered a real engineering organisation. Coding output rose 12.4%. Project management overhead dropped 24.9%. Those sound like wins — until you see that peer collaboration collapsed by nearly 80%. The time 'saved' from administrative work didn't become thinking time. It became solo screen time. The machine optimised the individual while hollowing out the collective. A separate MIT Sloan / Microsoft Research / GitHub study found gen AI tools slash programming time by 56%, yet HBR reports that managers are now 'struggling to keep up' with the resulting acceleration. The productivity boom is real — but management infrastructure wasn't built for this cadence.

Meanwhile, HBR's Aruna Ranganathan published a bracing counter-argument in early 2026: AI Does Not Reduce Work — It Intensifies It. The time AI frees up is immediately filled by higher expectations, more deliverables, tighter turnaround. The 'saved time' never materialises as slack. It materialises as faster throughput and higher volume.

MIT Sloan Management Review adds another dimension. Benjamin Laker argues in 'When Not to Use AI' that trust is the human currency of management. AI should draft timelines and generate slides — but it should not broker relationships, negotiate trade-offs, or make judgment calls that require shared belief. A separate piece in the same publication warns that AI systems can actually worsen human decision-making by affirming users' biases and disrupting workflows.

The upshot for a mid-career professional is this: time management is not a scheduling problem. It is a sovereignty problem — deciding what not to do, whose expectations to decline, which meetings to kill. AI can absorb the overhead (McKinsey shows it eliminates bias from scheduling and cuts managerial bandwidth), but only if you know where to draw the line. Deploy it on tasks. Protect the relationships. The leverage is in the boundary, not the speed.
